stories.title: Mandatory RE quotas for data centres brighten outlook for solar developers
stories.summary: The government is preparing to impose a mandatory 30 percent renewable energy requirement on data center operations, a policy shift that would compel operators to source clean power and has generated industry discussion about what qualifies as off-grid renewable supply.
stories.why_it_matters: Mandatory RE quotas would fundamentally alter data center economics in APAC markets where grid renewable penetration remains low, forcing operators to negotiate directly with solar and wind developers for dedicated capacity or invest in on-site generation—creating procurement advantages for vertically integrated players with balance sheet depth while potentially excluding smaller colocation providers unable to secure long-term power purchase agreements.

stories.summary_zh: 政府正准备对数据中心运营实施强制的30%可再生能源要求，这一政策转变将迫使运营商采购清洁电力，并引发了关于什么构成off-grid可再生能源供应的行业讨论。
stories.why_zh: 强制可再生能源配额将根本改变可再生能源电网渗透率仍然较低的亚太市场的数据中心经济学，迫使运营商直接与太阳能和风能开发商谈判获取专用容量或投资现场发电——这为具有资产负债表深度的垂直整合玩家创造采购优势，同时可能排除无法 securing 长期购电协议的较小colocation提供商。
stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 9, 2026 - November 15, 2026

A series of developments is lifting the prospects of solar farm developers as the government seeks to increase renewable energy (RE) adoption in the power-hungry data centre (DC) sector.

Last month, Minister of Energy Transition and Water Transformation Datuk Amar Fadillah Yusof said the government was drafting a framework for DC power consumption, which includes a minimum RE requirement of 30%.

Sources tell The Edge that the government is exploring even higher RE targets for future DC projects, particularly those powered off-grid.

It is understood that the 30% threshold has been floated since earlier this year. For DCs approved on the condition of using off-grid power, talk is that the RE requirement could go as high as 50%, although specific details are still being ironed out.

If implemented, the compulsory RE requirements could catalyse new solar farm developments under the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS), which allows RE developers to sell electricity directly to industrial customers.

CRESS adoption has been moving slowly because its primary target market, the DCs, are weighing the programme’s total cost — how much one pays for solar energy plus fees to use Tenaga Nasional Bhd’s (KL:TENAGA) grid — against the cost of just drawing electricity directly from the grid via Tenaga.

A mandatory RE quota now leaves DCs with no choice but to comply and look for solar farms to partner with.

“Thirty per cent is a good number for the DCs. The requirement could be more after that,” says a source.

According to the latest publicly available data, CRESS has attracted the interest of 11 solar farm developers and eight end-consumers, representing more than 3gw in capacity.

One CRESS project making advanced progress is a 100mw solar farm under construction in Kedah, led by privately owned HLGY Energy Sdn Bhd and Singapore-headquartered Bridge Data Centres.

Recent CRESS awards include two projects totalling 189mw won by Northern Solar Holdings Bhd (KL:NORTHERN). Meanwhile, Tenaga is reportedly exploring a 500mw solar supply arrangement with DayOne DCs.

Nevertheless, some power generation developers remain cautious about CRESS’ prospects. “I won’t celebrate yet, not until we see \[the conditions\] in an official document,” says an executive, pointing to recent adjustments in grid usage fees under CRESS.

In September, the Ministry of Energy Transition and Water Transformation (Petra) announced a reduction in the System Access Charges (SAC) to 14 sen/kWh, down from 20 sen previously, for eligible participants. However, the Energy Commission then clarified in October that CRESS projects remain subject to an additional charge of 4 sen/kWh.

When asked whether a mandatory RE requirement will slow down DC projects, industry players suggest that approved DCs yet to begin construction will likely proceed. A more decisive factor to look at is the government’s push for DCs to source their own electricity off-grid, they say.

How much RE generation capacity needs to be planted up depends on the details in the upcoming framework.

Should the 30% RE requirement be based on gigawatt-hour (gwh) — the total energy consumed over a certain period — a solar farm’s peak generation capacity must be between 80% and 90% bigger than the DC’s capacity to meet the 30% requirement due to the intermittency of solar energy production. For example, a 100mw data centre would roughly require a 180mwp solar farm to meet its 30% RE energy consumption target.

Data from the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) shows that the government has approved 23gw to 23.5gw of DC capacity, based on maximum demand. This includes 27 DCs that are expected to use off-grid electricity, which reports say carry a combined capacity of about 8gw.

As at August, operational DCs had contracted 2.3gw in capacity demand. By 2030, the total maximum DC demand is expected to cross 8gw, potentially requiring 14gwp of RE capacity to meet a 30% energy supply rule.

Nevertheless, the devil is in the details. Among the questions raised by industry players are whether programmes like CRESS is eligible to be considered as off-grid supply for DCs, or only dedicated self-consumption (Selco) solar installations qualify. Selco solar projects are more challenging logistically because they must be located close to the consumption point.

Another question is whether the Green Electricity Tariff (GET) — RE sold by Tenaga through the grid at a slight premium to the normal tariff — qualifies as RE for the DCs.

GET supply totalling 6.6TWh has been fully taken up, according to data from the Malaysia Green Attribute Tracking System (mGATS). Based on existing available RE capacity of nearly 6gw on the grid, back-of-the-envelope calculations indicate that the GET quota could easily be expanded.

If that quota is increased and is allowed to qualify for DCs’ mandatory 30% RE target, the GET could end up absorbing much of the demand from existing contracted DC capacity of 2.3gw.

One industry player views this outcome as unlikely, though, saying: “The government’s ultimate objective is new generation capacity. But nothing is official yet.”

Outside the DC space, rising fossil fuel costs continue to favour RE adoption.

Malaysia’s electricity tariff has incorporated a fuel surcharge since May, which official projections indicate will stabilise at a higher level in the coming months, potentially increasing to 6 to 8 sen/kWh based on the latest official projections.

Against this backdrop, CRESS is being explored by other industrial users. Among them is a major 680mw joint development between Gamuda Bhd (KL:GAMUDA), SD Guthrie Bhd (KL:SDG) and Petroliam Nasional Bhd’s (PETRONAS) Gentari Sdn Bhd for a US-based tech firm.

The appetite for rooftop solar has picked up again. Data from the Sustainable Energy Development Authority (Seda) shows more than 490mw in rooftop solar applications were submitted in the first 10 months of 2026, with 307mw already operational.

For solar developers, the momentum shows no sign of slowing. Malaysia’s latest Large-Scale Solar bidding round (LSS6) concluded in late October, offering a total allocation of 2,650mw, with the winning bids expected to be announced as early as January next year.

stories.summary: KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 17): Malaysia's integrated circuit (IC) design industry could face additional regulatory hurdles under the US' new export controls on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, particularly companies serving non-US customers developing advanced chips, although the direct impact on design services remains limited for now, according to Kenanga Research.

stories.title_zh: 美国芯片限制加大马来西亚IC设计行业风险，数据中心需求保持坚挺——Kenanga
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 17): Malaysia's integrated circuit (IC) design industry could face additional regulatory hurdles under the US' new export controls on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, particularly companies serving non-US customers developing advanced chips, although the direct impact on design services remains limited for now, according to Kenanga Research.

In a strategy note on Tuesday, the research house said the new US interim final rule (IFR) introduces licensing requirements for advanced logic chips designed by companies that are not approved or authorised IC designers.

While IC design services are not directly prohibited, the rules could affect downstream manufacturing and the delivery of finished chips, warranting closer monitoring.

The rules also retain the worldwide scope of the advanced computing foreign direct product rule, meaning qualifying foreign-produced chips could remain subject to US export controls.

The new IFR takes a two-pronged approach, tightening controls on remote access to advanced computing capacity and introducing licensing requirements for transferring advanced semiconductors to countries including Malaysia.

The measures are aimed at preventing Chinese technology firms from circumventing US chip export restrictions by accessing computing power through overseas cloud providers and data centres.

Under the rules, a destination-based licence is required for the export, re-export or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

The restrictions also cover overseas data centres that remotely provide significant volumes of computing capacity to companies headquartered in countries under the US' D:5 export control category, including China and Macau.

Kenanga said the new rules were less punitive than the Joe Biden-era AI diffusion rule, which divided countries into tiers and imposed country-level quotas.

Despite tighter regulatory scrutiny, Kenanga expects Malaysia's data centre demand to hold up, supported by US hyperscalers seeking overseas capacity as regulatory and approval uncertainties grow in several US states.

It noted that Malaysia has a 12.3 gigawatt (GW) data centre project pipeline with secured electricity supply, providing strong visibility for future development.

US-headquartered companies are exempt from the new rule, limiting the immediate impact on Kenanga's construction coverage universe, whose clients are predominantly US-based hyperscalers such as Google, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft.

As such, the research house considers the recent sell-off in core-and-shell engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) stocks excessive.

Gamuda Bhd (KL:GAMUDA) and Sunway Construction Group Bhd (KL:SUNCON) stand out as its safest picks given their predominantly US clientele.

"Overall, data centre demand in Malaysia remains strong but we believe that the demand will be focused more on US-based customers or non-China-linked players," it said.

Kenanga identified Sunway Construction's RM748 million project with K2 Strategic Infrastructure Malaysia Sdn Bhd, a non-US customer, as the only potential exception. However, the contract is relatively small and nearing completion, making any financial or operational impact on the group essentially remote.

Within the utilities sector, Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) is largely shielded by five-year take-or-pay clauses in its electricity supply agreements.

For YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR), Kenanga said it had not priced in any Neo cloud valuation beyond announced plans, leaving its earnings forecasts unchanged. Its colocation expansion could also capture spillover demand from US customers, although client onboarding may become more selective.

Meanwhile, mechanical and electrical (M&E) contractors face greater near-term risks as stricter end-use verification and graphics processing unit (GPU) licensing requirements could delay projects involving non-US operators without confirmed customers.

With the sector trading at about 13 times forward FY2028 price-earnings ratio, valuations may remain subdued pending greater visibility on new contracts.

Kee Ming Group Bhd (KL:KEEMING) remains Kenanga's top M&E pick, with an 'outperform' rating and a target price of RM3.23, supported by its diversified order book and greater exposure to US hyperscalers.

stories.summary: Nvidia has privately warned customers and partners that proposed US legislation targeting Chinese companies' remote access to its AI chips could expose both the chipmaker and buyers to legal action, according to a CNBC report citing sources familiar with the communications.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia's legal risk warnings force APAC distributors, cloud providers, and enterprise buyers to scrutinize their contractual indemnification and compliance architectures, as the company appears to be shifting potential liability downstream—creating a chilling effect on secondary market transactions and gray-market GPU access routes that have proliferated across Southeast Asia since initial export controls.

stories.content:
(Nov 17): Nvidia said in recent months a proposed US legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial intelligence chips could expose it and them to US "legal action," *CNBC* reported on Tuesday, citing sources.

*Reuters* could not immediately verify the report.

Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or Rasa, would give the US government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, the report said

The chipmaker said for now it would not sell chips to customers who rent over 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs to Chinese companies, the report added

Nvidia did not immediately respond to *Reuters*' request for comment outside regular business hours

Rasa is a bill that would give the US Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips.

The company said in July that the measure, if enacted, could have "a material impact on our business".

stories.title: Data centre, cloud computing investments surge 44.5% to RM123.5b in first nine months of 2026
stories.summary: Malaysia approved RM123.5 billion in data center and cloud computing investments during the first nine months of 2026, a 44.5 percent year-on-year increase that raised the sector's share of total approved investments to 35.2 percent from 29.4 percent previously.
stories.why_it_matters: Malaysia's investment surge intensifies competition with Singapore and Indonesia for APAC data center capital, but the concentration of approvals raises questions about power grid readiness and renewable energy availability in Johor and Kuala Lumpur corridors—if infrastructure cannot match the investment pace, Malaysia risks project delays or stranded capacity that could redirect hyperscale demand back to more established hubs.

stories.title_zh: 2026年前九个月数据中心和云计算投资激增44.5%至1235亿令吉
stories.summary_zh: 2026年前九个月，马来西亚批准的数据中心和云计算投资达1235亿令吉，同比增长44.5%，使该行业占批准投资总额的比重从29.4%上升至35.2%。
stories.why_zh: 马来西亚的投资激增加剧了其与新加坡和印尼争夺亚太数据中心资本的竞争，但批准的集中引发了对柔佛和吉隆坡走廊电力基础设施就绪性和可再生能源可用性的质疑——如果基础设施无法匹配投资节奏，马来西亚可能面临项目延迟或闲置产能风险，导致hyperscale需求回流至更成熟的枢纽。
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 17): Investments in data centres and cloud computing in Malaysia surged 44.5% year-on-year to RM123.5 billion across 86 approved projects in the first nine months of 2026, accounting for 35.2% of total approved investments, up from 29.4% a year earlier.

The investments formed a significant portion of the services sector, which attracted RM219.1 billion in approved investments, up 14.2% from RM191.7 billion a year earlier, according to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) on Tuesday (Nov 17).

The information and communications subsector, which includes data centre and cloud computing activities, led services investment approvals at RM133.5 billion, followed by real estate at RM47.9 billion, support services at RM19.3 billion, utilities at RM5.8 billion and distributive trade at RM5.1 billion.

To encourage local participation, Mida requires new data centres to meet a minimum of 30% local content.

Overall, Malaysia's approved investments rose 20.7% year-on-year to RM350.4 billion in the nine-month period, driven by a 40.7% increase in foreign investment approvals to RM212.3 billion, which accounted for 60.6% of the total.

Domestic investment approvals edged down 1% to RM138.1 billion.

The US was the largest source of foreign investments, with approvals surging more than fivefold to RM60 billion from RM11.3 billion a year earlier. This was followed by China (RM38.6 billion), Singapore (RM38.5 billion), Japan (RM24.4 billion) and Australia (RM12.6 billion).

The top five countries collectively accounted for 82% of total approved foreign investments.

The 4,387 approved projects are expected to generate more than 152,000 jobs, particularly in high-value sectors such as chip design, advanced electronics and precision engineering.

Mida chairman Tengku Datuk Seri Zafrul Abdul Aziz said in the statement that the agency was working with industry and education partners to ensure talent development kept pace with investors' needs.

Meanwhile, approved investments in the manufacturing sector rose 13.3% year-on-year to RM106.3 billion across 1,353 projects, reversing a 25.1% contraction in the first half of the year.

The recovery was supported by major third-quarter investment approvals involving the production of optical transceivers for artificial intelligence (AI) data centres and liquefied natural gas processing.

The electrical and electronics (E&E) industry led manufacturing investment approvals, with investments jumping 85.3% to RM40.8 billion, followed by petroleum products including petrochemicals at RM13.2 billion, machinery and equipment at RM9.4 billion, basic metal products at RM6.7 billion and food manufacturing at RM6.4 billion.

Domestic manufacturing investments surged 82.7% to RM37.8 billion while foreign manufacturing investments amounted to RM68.5 billion.

Approved manufacturing projects are expected to generate 92,489 jobs, up 27.3% from 72,672 a year earlier, with 78% of the positions allocated to Malaysians. Some 16,607 jobs are expected to offer monthly salaries of RM5,000 and above.

Johor attracted the highest approved investments in the nine-month period at RM99.7 billion, followed by Selangor at RM87.9 billion, Penang at RM41.1 billion, Kuala Lumpur at RM37.3 billion and Sabah at RM19.5 billion.

Foreign investments accounted for 81.7%, or RM81.4 billion, of Johor's total approvals, the highest proportion among the five leading investment destinations.

Selangor recorded the highest number of approved projects at 1,302 and the most expected jobs at 34,971 while Penang led in expected manufacturing employment with 26,643 jobs.

On project implementation, Mida said 87.4% of the 6,202 manufacturing projects approved between 2021 and September 2026 had reached various stages of production, factory construction or machinery installation.

Another 9.5% remained in the planning stage while 3.1% had yet to be implemented.

As at October, Mida had 223 proposed investment projects worth RM41.2 billion in its pipeline, comprising 119 manufacturing projects worth RM18.6 billion and 104 services projects worth RM22.6 billion.

The agency was also in discussions over potential investments worth a further RM60.5 billion.

Mida CEO Datuk Sikh Shamsul Ibrahim Sikh Abdul Majid said investment approvals needed to translate into actual economic activity.

"Approval is an important milestone but implementation is what delivers factories, business activities and jobs," he said.

stories.title: Chinese AI stocks down as US chip curbs hit labs and hyperscalers
stories.summary: Chinese AI-related stocks fell sharply following tightened US semiconductor export controls, with major domestic hyperscalers and AI model developers including Alibaba, Baidu, and ByteDance affiliates suffering significant losses as their access to advanced training chips faces further constraints.
stories.why_it_matters: The market reaction accelerates China's push for domestic GPU alternatives and may redirect Chinese AI training demand toward APAC third-party data centers in jurisdictions with less explicit US technology restrictions, though the remote access rule closes some avenues—Southeast Asian operators must now assess whether serving Chinese AI labs' inference workloads is commercially viable without triggering secondary sanctions exposure.

stories.title_zh: 美国芯片限制打击实验室和hyperscaler，中国AI股票下跌
stories.summary_zh: 美国半导体出口管制收紧后，中国AI相关股票大幅下跌，包括阿里巴巴、百度和字节跳动关联公司在内的主要国内hyperscalers和AI模型开发商遭受重大损失，因其获取先进训练芯片的渠道面临进一步限制。
stories.why_zh: 市场反应加速了中国对国产GPU替代品的推动，并可能将中国的AI训练需求转向美国技术限制较不明确的亚太第三方数据中心，尽管远程访问规则关闭了一些渠道——东南亚运营商现在必须评估服务中国AI实验室的推理工作负载是否具有商业可行性，而不会触发次级制裁风险。
stories.content:
(Nov 17): Chinese artificial-intelligence (AI) stocks tumbled on Tuesday after the US moved to further restrict access to advanced chips, with the country’s biggest hyperscalers and AI model developers among the hardest hit.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd shares dropped as much as 5.6% in Hong Kong while Baidu Inc’s tumbled 6.6%, helping drag the Hang Seng Tech Index down 2.3%. AI model pure plays Minimax Group Inc and Z.AI Co, or Zhipu, fell more than 6% each, while robot maker Yushu Technology Co sank as much as 11% in Shanghai.

The broad sell-off underscores how tighter US restrictions threaten multiple layers of China’s AI industry, from cloud giants supplying computing power to model developers racing to catch up with US rivals. The proposed rules could raise the cost of accessing advanced compute and close off overseas routes Chinese firms have used to work around existing restrictions.

“We see this as a negative development for China’s AI cloud industry, as tighter access to advanced computing resources could constrain AI model training and slow cloud revenue growth,” Nomura Holdings Inc analysts Jialong Shi and Rachel Guo wrote in a note.

The draft regulation would require data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a US government license before exporting advanced chips to customers in those countries. That would go a step beyond existing restrictions that prevent Chinese tech firms from directly buying some of the most advanced US chips.

The new rule was released days after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s chief executive officer following his admission to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Tech investors remain on edge with key earnings also due this week from Nvidia as well as Alibaba and Tencent Holdings Ltd.

“The curbs add a concrete risk to revenues and access to computing capacity, but they are landing in a market already nervous about AI valuations, spending returns and Nvidia’s leadership outlook,” said Charu Chanana, the chief investment strategist of Saxo Markets. “This is a meaningful escalation.”

The fallout extended beyond China. Samsung Electronics Co fell as much as 3.3% and Advantest Corp slid 6.3%, extending losses among Asian technology hardware shares already under pressure from the turmoil surrounding Nvidia and persistent concerns over AI financing.

“Tighter restrictions could raise concerns about slowing sales growth and may weigh on earnings in the short term” for Asian chip-related firms, said Hideyuki Ishiguro, the chief strategist of Nomura Asset Management. Some investors may also be selling holdings to raise cash ahead of the initial public offering of Anthropic PBC.

Southeast Asian stocks exposed to the AI build-out also came under pressure. Malaysia’s YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR), which has benefited from expectations of surging electricity demand from data centres, slumped nearly 10%.

Chinese chipmakers were a notable exception, as investors bet tighter US restrictions will accelerate the shift toward home-grown technology. Hong Kong-listed shares of Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp climbed as much as 6.4% while Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor Ltd surged 12%.

stories.summary: Any developments related to Nvidia do not significantly change Malaysia’s position of continuing to strengthen the semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) sectors, said Minister of Economy Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir.

stories.content:
PUTRAJAYA (Nov 17): Any developments related to Nvidia do not significantly change Malaysia’s position of continuing to strengthen the semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) sectors, said Minister of Economy Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir.

Akmal Nasrullah said Malaysia remains focused on investing in high-growth and high-value sectors, including semiconductors and AI, to create added value and better returns for the country.

He said issues related to Nvidia are now being handled at the level of the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti), and from the perspective of national economic planning, the focus on two sectors remains.

“So far, it has not significantly changed anything or actually altered our position to continue promoting the semiconductor and AI sectors,” he told the media after attending the Ministry of Economy’s monthly gathering here on Tuesday.

The minister was asked to comment on the issue involving Nvidia and its impact on the country’s semiconductor sector.

Akmal Nasrullah elaborated that the growth of Malaysia’s manufacturing and semiconductor export sector is not directly related to the issue.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had previously emphasised that there is no indication that AI chips related to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue were exported from Malaysia.

Miti also said it has never granted any approval to Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, based in Singapore, or its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd.

According to Miti, Speedmatrix is a data centre tenant in Malaysia and has brought its own servers and AI chips into the country for its operations.

The ministry said it is working with the Royal Malaysian Customs Department to determine whether any of the chips have been re-exported to other countries and comply with Malaysian laws.

stories.title_zh: 数据中心相关公司MN Holdings、Critical Holdings暴跌近20%，因美国宣布新芯片出口管制
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 17): Shares of data centre-related infrastructure players MN Holdings Bhd (KL:MNHLDG) and Critical Holdings Bhd (KL:CHB) plunged nearly 20% on Tuesday, triggering an automatic suspension in intraday short selling (IDSS), amid concerns over tighter US export controls on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

MN Holdings fell as much as 65 sen or 19.35% to RM2.71, its lowest since July 14. The stock pared its losses to RM2.74 at the noon break, down 62 sen or 18.45%, with 19.08 million shares traded. At that price, the company had a market capitalisation of RM1.93 billion.

Critical Holdings dropped as much as 40 sen or 19.51% to RM1.65, with 2.74 million shares traded, valuing the company at RM674.71 million.

IDSS is automatically triggered when a stock's last traded price falls more than 15 sen or 15% below its reference price. Short selling for both counters will resume at 8.30am on Wednesday.

The sell-off followed new US export controls tightening China's access to advanced AI chips. The rules require licences for the export, re-export or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, raising concerns over potential disruptions to the chip supply chain.

The requirements also compel data centres, foreign foundries and chip exporters to conduct enhanced due diligence on customers, including checks on direct or indirect ownership or control by entities in US-embargoed destinations or Macau.

MN Holdings and Critical Holdings are among the engineering and infrastructure companies supporting Malaysia's growing data centre and high-voltage infrastructure market.

The broader technology sector also came under pressure, with the Bursa Malaysia Technology Index falling more than 6% on Tuesday.

An analyst said the new US requirements could delay data centre projects as operators assess the implications of the licensing rules.

"Notably, the previous AI diffusion rule had delayed data centre project awards by six to seven months.

"We expect near-term sentiment pressure across power infrastructure names, although contractors with more diversified order books and lower data centre concentration should be relatively less affected," the analyst added.

stories.title: MyDCD expects maintenance revenue growth as data centre projects reach completion
stories.summary: MyDCD Bhd (KL:MYDCD) expects its maintenance revenue to grow as more data centre projects reach completion, while pursuing opportunities to service facilities built by other contractors.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: MyDCD预计随着数据中心项目完工，维护收入将增长
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 17): MyDCD Bhd (KL:MYDCD) expects its maintenance revenue to grow as more data centre projects reach completion, while pursuing opportunities to service facilities built by other contractors.

“We expect maintenance revenue to increase progressively as more of our ongoing projects are completed and transition into the maintenance phase,” MyDCD chief executive officer Chris Ow Yong said.

The engineering services company posted RM19.8 million in maintenance revenue for the financial year ended June 30, 2026 (FY2026) — a small fraction of its total revenue of more than RM666 million for the year.

Moving forward, growth would be supported by the increasing number of data centres in Malaysia and its growing portfolio of completed projects, it said, without providing a growth target.

“Beyond our existing projects, we also see potential opportunities in the broader data centre maintenance market, including both new and existing facilities, and will continue to evaluate such opportunities as they arise," said Ow Yong in a follow-up call with *The Edge.*

WATCH: MyDCD on building long-term customer relationships

Earlier, at MyDCD’s ACE Market listing ceremony, Ow Yong told reporters that maintenance services allowed the group to retain customers beyond project delivery.

“After completing the build, then we continue to do maintenance. That’s why our customer back in 2011 is still our customer today,” he said.

Ow Yong added that the group also sees opportunities to maintain data centres it did not build.

At end-September, MyDCD had RM53.08 million in outstanding maintenance services and parts orders, expected to be recognised progressively through FY2032.

These formed part of its RM1.32 billion outstanding order book. The remaining RM1.27 billion comprised data centre engineering integration work, expected to be recognised progressively through FY2028.

MyDCD specialises in mechanical, electrical, plumbing and fire protection engineering services, primarily for data centres. Its services include engineering support, installation, testing and commissioning, as well as preventive and corrective maintenance.

Separately, Ow Yong attributed the group’s stronger first-quarter profit margin to value engineering work on its projects.

MyDCD posted net profit of RM25.71 million on revenue of RM178.68 million for the first quarter ended Sept 30, 2026 (1QFY2027), translating into a net profit margin of 14.4%, compared with approximately 10% for the full FY2026.

Ow Yong said earnings could fluctuate between quarters but did not provide a margin target for the rest of FY2027.

The group raised RM187.6 million through its initial public offering (IPO), with RM134 million allocated for working capital and RM39.9 million for business expansion. Another RM5 million is earmarked for information technology upgrades, followed by RM8.7 million for listing expenses.

MyDCD opened at 48 sen on Tuesday, eight sen or 14.3% below its IPO price of 56 sen, valuing the company at RM861.12 million.

stories.summary: The US Department of Justice has escalated a criminal investigation into Singapore-based Megaspeed, a cloud and AI infrastructure provider, for suspected semiconductor export control violations. stories.content:
The US Department of Justice is continuing its criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore based cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure provider, over suspected semiconductor export control violations, following an initial probe by the Department of Commerce in 2024. The investigation is now being led by the Department of Justice (DOJ) with assistance from the Department of Commerce (DOC) which began after authorities detected suspicious activity involving potential semiconductor diversion.

In a joint statement, the two departments indicated that they would pursue any criminal conduct uncovered during the investigation. However, they did not disclose specific allegations against Megaspeed, identify the suspected destination of any potentially diverted semiconductors or indicate whether charges had been filed.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” they said. “Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America’s technological edge.”

#### **How the investigation unfolded**

Shedding light on how things transpired, the DOC and DOJ’s statement said that in May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia regarding direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia added the Singaporean company to its “no sell” list, barring further sales while investigators from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), working with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site end-use inspection at Megaspeed’s premises.

Following the inspection, the DOJ assumed the lead role in the criminal investigation, while BIS continued to work with federal prosecutors on the case. The update comes amid increased scrutiny of suspected attempts to divert advanced semiconductors through third party companies to circumvent US export restrictions.

Referring to its previous track record of cracking down on semiconductor smuggling it said, “Under the Trump Administration, seventeen defendants across six separate investigations have been charged in connection with allegations of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of semiconductors.”

The Commerce Department has also increased monetary penalties in export control cases, describing the total as 18 times higher than during the Biden administration. The departments did not provide a timeline for the Megaspeed investigation or say whether additional enforcement actions were expected.

#### **Megaspeed says it will cooperate with investigations**

Just a few days before this, on November 12, Tan Yong Pong, Chairman & CEO, Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. had also made an official statement on the company website, saying, “Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government. Megaspeed has cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”

He also said, “To further reinforce our commitment to compliance, Megaspeed has retained a leading U.S. law firm to lead a comprehensive census of its graphics processing units (GPUs) and independently verify its export control compliance practices. Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws.”

stories.content:
Beijing is encouraging the use of distillation to make AI easier to deploy across the manufacturing sector

\[BEIJING\] Chinese entities are adopting increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American artificial intelligence models to train domestic rivals, documents show, as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and offset tightening US curbs on its access to chips.

A Reuters review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices and government documents reveals how the practice – known as distillation – has expanded beyond academic experiments into mainstream industrial use in China.

The records describe Chinese researchers using US models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models.

The documents also show that Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across China’s powerful manufacturing sector.

Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world.

While the process cannot reproduce a leading model’s full capabilities or eliminate the need for advanced computing power, it can help developers preserve selected skills in smaller systems that cost less to operate, potentially reducing their reliance on American technology.

China’s broadening use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American rivals.

Washington said on Monday (Nov 16) it would further restrict China’s access to such chips from companies like Nvidia.

Distillation is also a source of friction between the world’s two biggest economies ahead of the Nov 18 to 19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are expected to meet.

US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of aggressive, targeted distillation of American AI models on an industrial scale.

And at meetings in Chengdu in July, US Commerce Department officials raised concerns with Chinese regulators about developers collecting output from leading American AI models, warning that some activities could amount to intellectual property (IP) theft, three people familiar with the discussions said.

Chinese officials defended distillation as a standard AI-development technique and said they were open to acting where the conduct constituted IP theft, but made no concrete commitments, according to a US official familiar with the previously unreported exchange.

The US Commerce Department and China’s Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment.

## From American answers to Chinese models

Distillation involves a powerful “teacher” model generating answers or demonstrating how to complete tasks, which developers use to train a smaller “student” system.

For Chinese developers facing constraints on computing power, the attraction is in making one expensive query do repeated work, according to a former Alibaba Group engineer who spoke on condition of anonymity.

An American model can generate the answer to a difficult question once, allowing a Chinese team to retain useful examples and train a local system around them.

In a November 2024 paper, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers described selecting about 5,000 answers from OpenAI’s o1 model, translating them using GPT-4o mini and assembling 10,750 bilingual training examples to further train Alibaba’s Qwen2.5-72B model.

The researchers also cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation, leaving developers dependent on breakthroughs made by more advanced model providers.

The project illustrated how American model output can become reusable data, allowing developers to improve domestic systems without repeatedly consulting the original provider.

Alibaba researchers described a more systematic approach in an April 2025 paper, using OpenAI’s GPT-4 and GPT-4o to generate training material in languages other than Chinese, then refining and scoring responses before training smaller Qwen models.

In a February 2026 paper, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chinese food delivery company Meituan described using GPT-4o to generate plans for coordinating AI agents working together on programming problems, helping train a smaller model to organise such tasks.

Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment.

## A growing geopolitical dispute

Among leading American AI companies, OpenAI’s terms restrict using its output to develop competing models, subject to exceptions, while Anthropic similarly restricts training competing systems without permission.

A US official familiar with the July Chengdu regulatory discussions said Washington believes industrial-scale distillation is the main reason Chinese AI models have narrowed the gap with their American rivals.

Two people familiar with Chinese developers’ operations disputed that assessment, saying distillation was only one factor alongside advances in engineering, algorithms, data and model design.

Chinese government documents do not instruct companies to distil American models but encourage distillation as part of Beijing’s push to spread AI across the world’s second-largest economy.

A national AI+Manufacturing policy package published by eight Chinese government agencies in January includes guidance supporting model training, fine-tuning and distillation for industrial applications.

Shanghai and Shenzhen have also encouraged techniques to reduce computing requirements.

The policies reflect Beijing’s ambition to deploy smaller, cheaper AI systems across industries.

Concerned by distillation’s growing geopolitical sensitivities, Chinese AI developers have in recent months asked Beijing’s industry regulator for guidance on the boundaries between ordinary use of foreign models and organised collection of output for training, according to one person familiar with the discussions.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

stories.title: China's top AI firms limit cyber capabilities in latest models
stories.summary: The moves follow a series of signals from China’s government about the risks posed by AI
stories.title_zh: 中国顶级AI公司限制最新模型的网络能力
stories.content:
The moves follow a series of signals from China’s government about the risks posed by AI

CHINA’S top AI developers are releasing advanced models with reduced offensive cyber capabilities, stifling their ability to aid online attacks following a government proposal to ban such technology from being exported.

Recent models from Alibaba Group, Tencent and Moonshot AI have featured scaled-down offensive abilities and improved defensive aptitude. Alibaba unveiled the latest edition of its flagship Qwen series without its weights, the internal settings that shape how a model responds, preventing users from downloading and customising the model’s full version.

So-called open-weight systems are attractive to hackers because they can run them locally and configure their settings. DeepSeek’s models have proved particularly popular, while Alibaba’s Qwen series has been ranked among the most downloaded open-weight model families in the world.

For months, US AI companies have also been restricting access to their most cyber-capable systems. Anthropic PBC has kept its Mythos Preview model out of general release, making it available to selected organisations for defensive security work.

Last month, researchers at CrowdStrike Holdings said hackers used DeepSeek’s model to carry out attacks against organisations in 14 countries.

“The cyber ability of models, and soon the bio ability of the models, will reach a threshold where it’s actually possible to do harm,” said Yao Shunyu, Tencent’s chief AI scientist who previously worked for OpenAI, at an event this month in Hong Kong.

Tencent reduced cyber functions from its Hy4 model before releasing it earlier this month. Moonshot took a similar approach with its Kimi K3.1 Pro model, while Z.AI carried out security reviews and alerted organisations to system vulnerabilities before making its GLM-5.3 system open-weight in August.

The moves follow a series of signals from China’s government about the risks posed by AI.

Last month, China’s Ministry of Commerce unveiled plans for an export ban on AI tools capable of attacking critical national infrastructure, attacking government networks or threatening military targets.

Under the draft proposal, large language models deemed “world-leading” could also face restrictions on overseas deployment.

In early November, China’s top economic planner said it was accelerating the rollout of new safety standards and ethical guidelines for AI developers.

An official at the National Development and Reform Commission said there’s now a broad consensus about the opportunities and risks of AI, and that the country intends to embed security measures during the development process.

“China is trying to strike a balance between international commercialisation and strategic control of its AI technologies,” said Charles Li, chief analyst at TeamT5, an organization that tracks Asia Pacific cyber activity. “As Chinese frontier models reportedly narrow the gap with their US counterparts in cybersecurity capabilities, Beijing increasingly views these capabilities as strategic assets that warrant tighter export controls.”

In the US, AI products were linked to a spate of autonomous cyberattacks in recent months, raising concerns about the technology’s ability to carry out offensive operations without human oversight.

Over the summer, American firms Anthropic PBC and OpenAI reported incidents in which their models eluded security controls and attacked third-party websites.

The spate of incidents alarmed researchers and government leaders, prompting calls for more rigorous safety screening and more secure testing environments.

In collaboration with the US government, Anthropic has allowed a select group of organisations to test the cyber abilities of its most advanced systems.

Chinese AI models have raised similar fears, with Moonshot’s Kimi K3 breaking out of a testing environment from the UK government’s AI Security Institute.

Though the model did not try to breach other companies’ websites, as in some of the other episodes, the test showed it lacks cybersecurity controls, researchers said at the time.

Stripping cyber offence materials from training is a good way to make it harder for bad actors to use open-weight models to do harm, said Xiaojian Li, founder of AI safety firm Fangcun AI.

“It’s a good balance between cost and effectiveness, but it’s not perfect,” he said. “There is no such method now that can completely eliminate models’ risk.” BLOOMBERG

stories.content:
David Knox, Global Director of Energy & Sustainability at Colt Data Centre Services, argues that reliable power must shape data centre site selection from the outset.Grid connection queues are growing, and AI demand is accelerating faster than local power networks can deliver. This forces developers to rethink where, when, and how new capacity is built.The UK government reported a 460 per cent increase in power grid connection queues in six months. This rise is linked to a significant increase in speculative applications.AI data centres require several times the power density of traditional facilities. The number of operators seeking this level of capacity is growing.Most countries have sufficient power generation capacity to support AI data centre growth. However, local network constraints often mean demand exceeds what can be accommodated.Grid access is no longer a straightforward process. It is an ongoing negotiation that affects design assumptions and delivery risks from the outset.Organisations must prioritise flexibility in their grid access approach for AI data centres. This includes using modular power systems and hybrid supply models.Modular power systems support phased construction and energisation. This allows providers to respond more effectively to grid delays.Hybrid supply models can introduce additional power sources. They reduce reliance on the grid and improve resilience, acting as a capacity-bridging tool.Developers are rethinking location strategy for AI data centres. Competitiveness depends on certain power delivery and quick scaling.Historically, site selection focused on proximity to users, strong connectivity, and suitable land. Power was assumed to be available through standard grid connections.This assumption no longer holds. Many established data centre hubs have constrained or fully allocated grid capacity.Sites that appear ideal on paper can conceal significant delivery risks. These include long connection delays, complex network constraints, or substantial reinforcement costs.Developers must now balance traditional considerations with reliable power availability and scalability. The strongest location decisions prioritise speed to power, certainty of delivery, and long-term scalability.

stories.content:
Solar power continues to achieve historic milestones globally, with technological advancements driving efficiency gains.Perovskite solar cells, for instance, are boosting panel efficiency above 30 per cent, compared to the 22 per cent typical for standard panels. These tandem cells layer perovskite materials on silicon to capture different light wavelengths, converting more energy from the same footprint, according to industry analysts.Solar paired with energy storage now constitutes more than 70 per cent of all new United States generation capacity. This integration addresses the intermittency of solar power by storing excess energy for dispatch when needed, even at night.Data centers are driving significant growth in electricity demand, with some hyperscalers resorting to building their own fossil-fueled power plants for immediate needs, Lindsey Wiedmann, Chief Legal and Sustainability Officer at Nextpower, said. Utility-scale solar, combined with storage and intelligent controls, offers a fast and cost-effective way to add substantial new generation sustainably, Wiedmann added.Google, for example, is developing data centers alongside large-scale solar and battery storage projects in Haskell County, Texas, and Gray and Roberts counties, Texas. These projects, like Google's solar field in St. Ghislain, Belgium, integrate power generation into campus design, James Mercer of Metro Colo Advisory said.Developers are co-locating solar and storage facilities next to data centers to reduce grid connection wait times and alleviate strain on local grids, Mercer noted. The United States energy storage market saw a record 18.9 GW of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) installations in 2025, a 52 per cent increase over 2024, according to the American Clean Power Association and Wood Mackenzie.While recycling technologies for solar panels exist, more economical systems are needed to recover materials as electricity demand grows, Yagiz Sullu, founder and lead analyst at Sullu Strategic Advisory, said. Building a diversified and resilient electricity system is crucial rather than relying heavily on any single power source, Sullu added.

stories.title: Grid utilisation crucial for meeting AI electricity demand
stories.summary: Most energy industry decision-makers anticipate artificial intelligence (AI) driven electricity demand will exceed current forecasts. Optimising existing grid infrastructure through improved utilisation and flexible interconnection is crucial to meet this demand faster than building new lines. This approach impacts data center power strategies.
stories.title_zh: 电网利用率对满足AI电力需求至关重要
stories.content:
Most senior decision-makers in the energy industry expect artificial intelligence (AI) driven electricity demand to exceed current forecasts, according to a survey commissioned for ADIPEC. The poll found that 81 per cent of 1,528 respondents anticipate AI demand surpassing current projections, with 32 per cent expecting it to be much higher.A separate study by Jacobs, an engineering and consulting firm, highlights a capital and project gap. Among 600 energy-sector decision-makers across the U.S., U.K., Germany, Singapore, and Australia, 71 per cent reported sufficient capital availability in their regions. However, only 29 per cent indicated both enough capital and investable projects.Permitting and consenting were ranked among the top three biggest barriers by 80 per cent of respondents in the Jacobs study. ADIPEC's survey respondents identified delays in building and connecting grids as the second-biggest barrier to meeting demand, after geopolitics.
### Optimising Existing Infrastructure

State regulators are increasingly focusing on how much existing infrastructure can carry. The NC Clean Energy Technology Center's 50 States of Grid Modernization report for the third quarter of 2026 documented 411 grid modernization actions across 43 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. This tally includes dockets, proposals, and enacted policy, indicating significant activity.A key trend identified is the push for metrics and planning rules on "grid utilization," which measures how efficiently a utility uses its existing infrastructure. Virginia lawmakers were the first to mandate grid utilization metrics earlier this year, according to the report. California enacted a bill requiring public utility data on utilization opportunities and assessments of cost-effective solutions within distribution planning.Minnesota regulators directed Xcel Energy to incorporate utilization metrics into its next Integrated Distribution Plan. Colorado regulators initiated a rulemaking, requiring distribution system plans to include scenarios that use load flexibility to increase capacity utilization.Flexible interconnection is a practical approach to this. Xcel Energy has proposed offering both static and dynamic flexible interconnection in Colorado. This would allow customers to enroll temporarily until system upgrades are complete, or permanently as a long-term connection method.
### Advanced Transmission Technologies

New Jersey enacted a law mandating utilities to consider advanced transmission technologies in project applications. Third-party cost-effectiveness testing is required to justify any decision to exclude these technologies. Ohio regulators approved a cost-effectiveness methodology that accounts for reduced system losses and avoided upgrades.Indiana regulators also published a study covering nine categories of these technologies. Brian Lips, a senior project manager at the NC Clean Energy Technology Center, stated that policymakers are increasingly interested in advanced transmission technologies. These allow utilities to improve grid usage without replacing existing infrastructure.Statkraft, as cited in the Jacobs report, demonstrated this approach by shortening a battery project's connection timeline from seven years to two. This was achieved by examining network data, equipment capability, and operating conditions. The solution involved accepting that the facility could be curtailed during limited periods of genuine constraint.Will Hazelip, U.S. president of National Grid, noted in the Jacobs report that rapid load growth is diminishing system spare capacity. This creates a "resilience preparedness gap." The survey data suggests this gap is already evident, with 95 per cent of Jacobs' respondents confident in critical asset operation during disruptions. However, only 36 per cent described their resilience approach as proactive and embedded.

Regular testing failed to replicate the specific hardware and traffic conditions that eventually triggered the failure.A sudden surge in network traffic was the second factor. Teams had failed over from an alternative gateway to the primary gateway about 15 hours before the outage. This increased the load and altered traffic patterns on the primary gateway, making the latent software defect more likely to be triggered.The third factor was a nearly 14 per cent reduction in server capacity. This was due to an unrelated issue from the previous day. While not enough to disrupt services on its own, this reduced capacity contributed to the failure when combined with the other factors.The disruption escalated into a cascading failure as Microsoft's traffic management systems redirected requests from unavailable servers to healthy ones. The global deployment of the defect also prevented quick rollbacks.Engineers eventually identified the defect and developed an update. They applied the fix by taking groups of servers offline, updating them, and restarting them. This gradual restoration helped prevent overwhelming recovering servers.

stories.title: US-China split in strategic industries set to deepen as governments drive decoupling: Muzinich CEO
stories.summary: Spending on AI infrastructure will also fall in the longer term, he warns

stories.title_zh: Muzinich CEO：政府推动脱钩，中美战略产业分裂将加深
stories.content:
Spending on AI infrastructure will also fall in the longer term, he warns

\[SINGAPORE\] The US and China will likely become increasingly divided in strategic industries – such as artificial intelligence and rare earths – amid rising geopolitical tensions, said Justin Muzinich, CEO of private-debt specialist Muzinich.

As the two superpowers increasingly regard each other as strategic rivals, it is “rational” for both countries to want to separate when it comes to strategic dependencies going forward, he noted.

“The way I see the fault lines dividing is there will be a difference between strategic industries and non-strategic industries,” Muzinich said on Tuesday (Nov 17).

His comments come as the US announced new export controls on advanced AI semiconductor shipments to overseas data centres, following reports of these chips being illegally diverted to China through other countries, including Singapore.

Muzinich was speaking on a panel on investing in a fragmented world at the HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026. With him was George Yeo, former Singapore foreign minister and visiting scholar at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore.

The session was moderated by Barry O’Byrne, HSBC’s CEO of international wealth and premier banking.

Muzinich said both the US and China would prefer not to depend on each other for strategic industries, although this will not be the case for non-strategic sectors such as clothing exports.

In a separate interview with *The Business Times*, Muzinich noted that there is “still a lot of room for cooperation” in areas that are not considered as strategic, as both countries have an interest in sourcing the cheapest goods.

Meanwhile, the new export controls – which prevent China from renting capacity in third-party countries – were a foreseeable and “totally logical consequence” of the initial goal of preventing exports, he said.

“If you’re going to prevent the exports, you will probably also prevent circumventing those rules by allowing countries just to rent the space in third-party countries,” he added.

But while the US seemed determined to ban China’s access to Nvidia chips with the new export controls, Yeo does not expect this will restrict China. He said: “It’s clear that China’s AI development cannot be stopped.”

Muzinich said in the panel that, to separate strategic industries, the government will have to step in to force it from the top down.

“Companies ultimately care about the bottom line,” he pointed out. “The country should be willing to pay a cost, for instance, for having secure supply chains in strategic industries; private companies aren’t going to do that on their own.”

## AI infrastructure could slow

Separately, Muzinich warned that spending on AI infrastructure will fall in the longer term, especially since the world is spending “so much” on AI investments currently.

“There’s at least a decent probability that we’re in some sort of earnings bubble,” he said. “At some point, we’re going to have enough data centres for whatever AI people want to do, and we’re not going to need more, and revenue from all that will fall.”

He also expressed concern over mounting sovereign debt, especially in the US.

He said the US debt and deficit situation is “not sustainable”, with the US government unlikely to allow significant inflation, reduce spending or increase tax.

This could lead to a world where sovereigns are not considered the safest investments in the world in the next 10 years, with government yields surpassing corporate debt.

In the separate interview, Muzinich noted that corporate risk is not totally divorced from the government because governments can also influence corporates.

Nevertheless, he said the world is moving towards a time when it would be less risky to own a portfolio of diversified companies than one exposed to governments. Decision-makers in companies are rational and motivated by numbers, he explained, while governments may have high debt, and the decision-making may be driven by extreme politics.

He cited the example of Italy in 2012 to 2013, where corporates were doing well even amid sovereign risks.

“Markets can be pretty rational,” he said. “You’d much rather give money to corporates that have low debt levels.”

stories.title: GreenSquare commits to water stewardship standard for Sydney data centre
stories.summary: Australian data centre operator GreenSquare has committed to implementing the Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Standard, an international framework for responsible water management, at its SYD1 facility in western Sydney. The company announced the commitment on 17 November, saying it would work through the verification programme operated by Water Stewardship Asia Pacific (WSAP), which represents […]
stories.title_zh: GreenSquare承诺在悉尼数据中心实施水资源管理标准
stories.content:
Australian data centre operator GreenSquare has committed to implementing the Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Standard, an international framework for responsible water management, at its SYD1 facility in western Sydney.

The company announced the commitment on 17 November, saying it would work through the verification programme operated by Water Stewardship Asia Pacific (WSAP), which represents the Alliance for Water Stewardship in the region.

The AWS Standard assesses water management at both site and catchment level, covering water sources, on-site use and what happens to water after it leaves a facility. Its five outcomes address water governance, sustainable water balance, water quality, freshwater ecosystems and biodiversity, and access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene.

GreenSquare CTO Joshua Martens said the company’s water strategy began during site planning, with assessments of catchment water stress and available water sources informing facility design and location.

“Committing to the Alliance for Water Stewardship Standard is a natural step for GreenSquare, and it will give communities where we operate the confidence that we’re adhering to international best practice,” he said.

The commitment is being implemented at SYD1, a data centre in Norwest Business Park that became operational in October following the adaptive reuse of a facility originally built in 1995. GreenSquare claims SYD1 is designed to achieve a potable water usage effectiveness (WUE) of less than 0.1 litres per IT kilowatt-hour, compared with a NSW Government guideline benchmark of 1.0 litres per kWh.

The facility uses a closed-loop cooling system that operates without evaporative cooling for approximately 96 percent of the year, replacing the site’s previous water-intensive cooling towers. Rainwater harvesting is expected to meet around 10 percent of annual cooling water requirements.

According to GreenSquare, SYD1 is expected to use less water annually than the original data centre, despite increasing IT capacity by 275 percent. “We design our buildings to prioritise the use of harvested rain or recycled water while also ensuring every litre of potable water is used as efficiently as possible,” Martens said. “Importantly, this pledge shows GreenSquare is committed to transparency and to investigate ways to improve the local catchment areas where we operate.”

WSAP CEO Dr Sandra Hall said the commitment and independent verification would support greater transparency and accountability as Australia’s data centre industry expands. Under the commitment, GreenSquare will align its water stewardship work with existing catchment plans, engage with stakeholders and report on material water-related information. The company said the work at SYD1 would also inform the planning, design, construction and operation of future campuses.

stories.summary: Australian-based global data centre developer Goodman’s plans for an indicative 2,150 apartments in Macquarie Park in Sydney New South Wales have been declared State Significant Development, advancing a major residential proposal close to the company’s approved Project Apollo data centre. The residential development, proposed for 3–5 Talavera Road, comprises five towers ranging from 45 to […]
stories.title_zh: Goodman住宅计划与Macquarie Park数据中心同步推进
stories.content:
Australian-based global data centre developer Goodman’s plans for an indicative 2,150 apartments in Macquarie Park in Sydney New South Wales have been declared State Significant Development, advancing a major residential proposal close to the company’s approved Project Apollo data centre. The residential development, proposed for 3–5 Talavera Road, comprises five towers ranging from 45 to 60 storeys. The proposal includes a commitment to provide 4% affordable housing in perpetuity.

The residential proposal was formally declared State Significant Development on 27 October, following a recommendation by the Housing Delivery Authority. The declaration allows the project to proceed through the SSD assessment process but does not constitute development approval.

Goodman has planning consent for Project Apollo, a five-storey data centre at 4-10 Talavera Road. The AU$1.4 billion development has a planned capacity of 135MW and includes eight data halls, 66 backup generators and 36 cooling towers.

The proposed residential development is at 3-5 Talavera Road, while Project Apollo occupies 4–10 Talavera Road. The proximity of the two proposals has raised questions about how operational noise from the data centre, including its cooling plant and backup generators, will be considered in the assessment of the residential development.

It is understood Project Apollo underwent a detailed acoustic assessment as part of its planning and approval process, including consideration of operational noise from cooling plant and backup generators.

The acoustic material for Project Apollo identifies a number of existing noise-sensitive receiver locations, including residential properties in the surrounding area and the North Ryde Early Learning Centre on Talavera Road. The proposed residential tower site at 3–5 Talavera Road is not separately identified among those locations.

As a result, how noise from the data centre may affect future residents will be a question for the assessment of the residential project.

It is understood that any acoustic assessment or mitigation measures required for the residential proposal will be considered as it progresses through the planning process and in accordance with relevant requirements. It is not clear whether Goodman intends to undertake additional assessment or mitigation beyond those requirements.

The residential proposal remains at an early stage. The two projects are separate proposals within Macquarie Park, Sydney’s established employment and mixed-use precinct where housing, transport, commercial development and digital infrastructure are increasingly being planned alongside one another.

The residential project’s assessment will provide a further test of how the planning system considers the interface between large-scale data centre infrastructure and new housing, particularly where cooling plant and backup generation are part of an approved facility.

stories.title: Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia respond to new US chip export rule
stories.summary: Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia have begun formulating policy responses to a new US interim final rule from the Bureau of Industry and Security that further restricts China's access to advanced semiconductors through diversion controls and remote access limitations.
stories.why_it_matters: Southeast Asian governments now face pressure to align domestic cloud regulations with US extraterritorial controls or risk losing American chip technology access, while regional data center hubs must navigate conflicting commercial interests—hosting Chinese AI demand versus maintaining US technology partnerships—that could reshape competitive positioning across Singapore, Bangkok, and Jakarta.

stories.summary_zh: 新加坡、泰国和印尼已开始针对美国商务部工业与安全局(BIS)发布的新interim final rule制定政策回应，该规则通过转移管制和远程访问限制进一步限制中国获取先进半导体。
