stories.content:
The US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has moved to further restrict China’s potential access to advanced US semiconductor technology, cutting off avenues the country could use to divert chips and restricting remote access to US technology.

The new interim final rule (IFR) released on Monday November 16, 2026, outlines that exports of advanced US semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil will require a license. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in restricted countries or Macau as part of this new control.

In response to the IFR, Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) published a joint statement.

“We are studying the details of this new measure carefully. We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses. We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies,” the ministries said.

The MDDI and METI noted that they take Singapore’s international reputation seriously and do not condone companies using their association with it to circumvent or violate laws of other countries.

“As a global hub for technology and trade, Singapore will continue to safeguard the integrity of our business environment and continued access to advanced semiconductors and computing capabilities for legitimate companies operating here, and act against those who flout our laws,” the ministries added.

Indonesia’s Government Communication Agency told Bloomberg that government officials were reviewing the measure and looking to engage the industry for input as to any impact the IFR might have on operations and investment. The agency added that the government is working on a strategic trade management framework that enables legitimate trade while also reducing the risk that technology is diverted and misused.

Ahead of the announcement of the IFR, Thailand’s Vice Minister for Commerce Kirida Bhaopichitr told CNBC that the country was prepared for chip export restrictions. She said that Thailand would more carefully scrutinize chip importers to ensure those products aren’t being shipped to restricted countries via its market.

Brazil’s Ministry of Development, Industry, and Services said it was monitoring possible developments from the measure. It noted that the rule is not a ban on the export of advanced semiconductors to Brazil, but rather an authorization that now needs to take place. The ministry added that it’s not possible to evaluate the impact this would have on the import of US chips at this time.

The matter of chip diversion has come under scrutiny in recent weeks following an investigation into Singapore-based company Megaspeed. As w.media reported earlier today, the US Department of Justice together with the Department of Commerce intend to pursue any criminal conduct uncovered during the investigation. However, they did not disclose specific allegations against Megaspeed, identify the suspected destination of any potentially diverted semiconductors or indicate whether charges had been filed.

stories.title: Arbitrating data center disputes in Southeast Asia
stories.summary: Technology, obsolescence, and the neocloud challenge
stories.title_zh: 在东南亚仲裁数据中心争议
stories.content:
The four largest US hyperscalers have made a total of $1.1 trillion in capital expenditure on data centers, advanced chips, and the power to run them since the beginning of the AI boom in 2023.

This investment is not merely expanding capacity – it is fundamentally transforming the technological profile of what data centers must deliver. According to McKinsey research, traditional compute, storage, and cloud workloads have historically comprised over 70 percent of data center demand in Asia-Pacific, with AI training and inference contributing approximately 30 percent. That balance is expected to reach a roughly equal 50/50 split by 2030.

This technological shift creates a new category of disputes that permeates the entire project stack. Facilities designed for one generation of computing are being asked to support the next before construction is complete.

The pace of innovation is overtaking investment theses built on assumptions about technology lifecycles. For operators building and scaling hyperscale platforms across APAC, technological obsolescence risk is no longer a future concern – it is generating disputes today. This article examines how rapid technological change drives disputes and why arbitration, with its capacity to engage technically qualified decision-makers, offers the most effective forum for their resolution.

## **The five-year replacement cycle and investment horizon mismatch**

The servers powering AI workloads today may require significant upgrades or replacement within five years – a timeline that creates a fundamental misalignment with typical infrastructure investment horizons and depreciation models. Private equity sponsors typically underwrite data center investments on seven- to ten-year hold periods. Debt financing structures assume useful lives of fifteen to twenty years. Yet the computational infrastructure those investments support faces effective obsolescence on a cycle that is accelerating rather than stabilizing.

This misalignment gives rise to disputes between investors and operators. Where partnership agreements or shareholder agreements do not adequately address the pace of technological change, disagreements over capital expenditure obligations for technology refresh are inevitable. An investor expecting steady-state returns faces an operator requesting hundreds of millions in unbudgeted capital expenditure to remain competitive. Without express contractual mechanisms governing refresh obligations, trigger events, and cost allocation, these disagreements escalate rapidly into formal disputes.

## **The neocloud challenge**

Neocloud providers, specialised cloud platforms designed for high-performance computing workloads, emerged in 2023–2024 and rapidly gained traction through 2025. Their business model demands infrastructure specifications that substantially exceed what standard colocation agreements contemplate: rack densities exceeding 50kW, liquid cooling systems rather than traditional air cooling, and power redundancy configurations optimised for continuous high-intensity computation rather than variable enterprise workloads.

For operators, neocloud tenants represent both the highest-value customers and the most challenging to serve. Standard powered-shell agreements negotiated with enterprise tenants assume power densities of 8–15kW per rack and air-cooled environments. When a Neocloud customer requires 50kW or more per rack with direct liquid cooling, the gap between the contracted specification and actual demand creates immediate tension. Who bears the cost of the cooling retrofit? Does the powered-shell agreement require the operator to deliver infrastructure capable of supporting next-generation workloads, or only the specifications expressly stated at signing?

These questions are arising across the region as operators compete for the most valuable tenant relationships.

## **Design basis assumptions becoming obsolete during construction**

Perhaps the most commercially complex disputes arise when design basis assumptions become obsolete during the construction period itself. A hyperscale data center campus takes two to four years from design freeze to full commissioning. In Southeast Asia, where power connection lead times alone can exceed two years, total development timelines frequently stretch further. During that period, the technology landscape shifts materially.

An EPC contract executed in 2024 on the basis of 20kW average rack density may face a customer agreement signed in 2026 that contemplates 50kW rack density with liquid cooling. The EPC contractor has designed and is delivering to the original brief. The operator needs the facility to serve a customer whose requirements have evolved. This creates a three-way tension: the developer expects delivery to the original specification; the operator needs modifications to serve its tenant; and the EPC contractor contends that design changes constitute variations outside the contracted scope.

The question of whether specifications for new-build facilities should have anticipated current power density requirements – including rack densities exceeding 50kW – can drive claims for defective design or inadequate design life. Conversely, EPC contractors argue that they delivered to the brief provided, and that subsequent technology evolution is not a design deficiency. These disputes are technically complex, commercially significant, and increasingly common.

## **Disputes at every level of the project stack**

Technological obsolescence generates disputes at multiple levels simultaneously:

- **Between investors and operators:** Disagreements over capital expenditure obligations for technology refresh, particularly where the original investment thesis assumed stable infrastructure and steady-state returns.
- **Between operators and tenants:** Questions whether colocation or powered-shell agreements require the operator to upgrade infrastructure to support next-generation chip architectures – particularly where liquid cooling retrofits are needed and the original lease contemplated air-cooled facilities at lower power densities.
- **Between developers and EPC contractors:** Claims that design specifications should have anticipated higher power density requirements, or conversely that design changes during construction constitute compensable variations. Disputes over design life warranties and whether OCP Ready certification was within the contracted scope.
- **Between the EPC contract and the customer agreement:** Structural tension where the EPC contract reflects the original brief and the customer agreement contemplates technology evolution – with the operator caught between two incompatible sets of obligations.

## **Practical recommendations**

### First, address obsolescence risk expressly in the contracting suite

Technology refresh obligations, capital expenditure triggers, and the allocation of upgrade costs between operator and tenant should be expressly addressed across the project stack. Hyperscaler customer agreements should specify power density escalation pathways – for example, providing for staged increases from 20kW to 35kW to 50kW per rack with defined trigger mechanisms and cost-sharing arrangements. Cooling upgrade triggers should be contractually defined: at what tenant density threshold does the obligation to install liquid cooling systems arise, and who bears that cost?

### Second, build flexibility into EPC contracts

Design life warranties should address not merely structural longevity but functional relevance. EPC contracts should incorporate mechanisms for design evolution during the construction period – including defined variation procedures for power density increases, cooling system upgrades, and connectivity specifications. Where OCP Ready certification or equivalent standards are anticipated, they should be expressly within the contracted scope from the outset.

### Third, align investment documents with technology cycles

Partnership and shareholder agreements must address technology refresh as a foreseeable capital requirement rather than an extraordinary event. Reserved matters, capital call mechanics, and return calculations should all contemplate periodic refresh expenditure. Depreciation assumptions in financial models should reflect five-year technology replacement cycles rather than twenty-year building lifecycles.

### Fourth, select arbitration for technical disputes

Disputes involving PUE metrics under varying AI workload profiles, liquid cooling system specifications, OCP Ready certification requirements, and the engineering standards required for hyperscale operation demand adjudicators who can engage with technical evidence directly. SIAC arbitration allows parties to appoint arbitrators with specific engineering or technology expertise – a decisive advantage over national courts where judges may have no background in data center infrastructure. The ability to engage with complex evidence concerning rack densities, cooling coefficients, power redundancy configurations, and design life calculations enables more accurate and commercially informed outcomes.

Technological obsolescence is not a future risk for Southeast Asia's data center sector – it is generating disputes today. The pace of innovation in AI computing means that facilities designed for current workloads face functional obsolescence within their construction period. For operators managing the tension between investment commitments, EPC delivery, and tenant demands for next-generation infrastructure, the contracting suite must expressly address technology evolution rather than treating it as an unforeseeable contingency.

Arbitration's ability to appoint technically qualified arbitrators and engage with complex engineering evidence makes it the forum of choice for these disputes. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss how obsolescence risk can be addressed in your platform's contracting arrangements and how dispute resolution provisions can be calibrated to the technical complexity of these emerging claims.

*This industry view was co-written with Andrew Raymond, legal director in Singapore at Charles Russell Speechlys LLP*

stories.content:
The US Department of Commerce has issued an interim final rule (IFR) to restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and servers and added five new countries to its export restriction list.

Per a statement issued by the Bureau of Industry & Security (BIS), the new rule has been designed to ensure existing restrictions “cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

Data centers, overseas foundries, and chip exporters will be required to perform “robust due diligence on customers,” which includes ensuring they are not owned – either directly or indirectly – by persons on the US government’s restricted export list.

Additionally, under the new rule, licenses will now be required to export, reexport, or transfer in-country advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil – countries which the government deems to present “a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.”

However, the license requirement for those countries will not apply when the chips are destined for companies headquartered in, or have a parent company headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met.

The rule has been issued in the wake of the fallout from the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) was an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based IT and cloud company currently under investigation for smuggling Nvidia GPUs into China.

Following reports emerged that he had additionally engaged in an affair with a direct report, on November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and a member of the board with immediate effect after 33 years leading the company. Last week, US President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the incident.

“Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI (super intelligence) infrastructure has made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely,” BIS said in a statement. “This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.”

stories.title: Nvidia unveils Rubin HPC GPU for agentic AI-powered science and engineering workloads
stories.summary: Nvidia has unveiled a new GPU dubbed Rubin HPC, a chip supported by the company’s Vera Rubin platform.
stories.title_zh: NVIDIA发布面向agentic AI驱动的科学与工程工作负载的Rubin HPC GPU
stories.content:
Nvidia has unveiled a new GPU dubbed Rubin HPC, a chip supported by the company’s Vera Rubin platform.

Designed to support agentic AI-powered simulation and data processing workloads across science, engineering, and analytics, the chip giant said Rubin HPC will shorten the timeline between exploration and results.

Rubin HPC features more than 50,000 CUDA cores alongside a sparse data acceleration capability that accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation Nvidia NVLink interconnect technology.

Furthermore, instead of increasing compute capacity alone, Nvidia said the new chip offers a “balanced design” that scales data movement and compute together, which accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions, all of which are common across data analytics, science, and engineering workloads.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia.

“Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

stories.title: Singapore tops Southeast Asia data centre costs, says report
stories.summary: A new cost analysis report shows Singapore commanding the highest data center construction costs in Southeast Asia at $15.39 per watt, nearly double Ho Chi Minh City's $8.32 per watt, reflecting land scarcity, stringent regulations, and premium infrastructure standards in the city-state.
stories.why_it_matters: The cost divergence will drive workload tiering across APAC, with latency-sensitive financial services and sovereign data remaining in Singapore while bulk AI training and storage workloads migrate to lower-cost Vietnamese, Indonesian, and Malaysian markets—reshaping regional data center development patterns and potentially creating network infrastructure investment needs for inter-country latency optimization.

stories.content:
Mon, 16th Nov 2026 (Yesterday)
Singapore is Southeast Asia's most expensive market for data centre construction, according to Turner & Townsend, and ranks fourth globally at USD $15.39 per watt.

Construction costs vary widely across the region. Jakarta ranked 26th globally at USD $11.96 per watt, Kuala Lumpur and Johor Bahru were joint 49th at USD $10.06, Bangkok was 55th at USD $9.67, Manila 56th at USD $9.55, and Ho Chi Minh City 60th at USD $8.32.

The figures come from the latest edition of Turner & Townsend's Data Centre Construction Cost Index, which tracks 62 markets using a typical 60 MW design. It draws on more than 500 live or recently completed projects and a survey of more than 400 industry specialists.

Tokyo topped the global ranking for the fourth consecutive year at USD $18.28 per watt, followed by Osaka at USD $17.15. Zurich was third at USD $15.93, leaving Singapore behind only the two Japanese cities and the Swiss market.

Hong Kong was the next Asian market at 14th with USD $12.97 per watt. Lower-cost Asian markets outside Southeast Asia included Mumbai at USD $6.83 and Shanghai at USD $5.79, the cheapest location in the index.

### Regional spread

The rankings highlight how uneven Southeast Asia's market remains as developers weigh land, labour, utilities and supply chain access. Singapore's position reflects its maturity, while Vietnam remains among the cheapest places globally to build new data centre capacity.

"As surging demand for AI continues to drive the race to deliver data centre mega projects, the cost spread in Southeast Asia reflects the different stages of market maturity across the region. Singapore's position as an established hub brings higher land, labour and compliance costs, while emerging markets like Ho Chi Minh City offer lower build costs as infrastructure and supply chains continue to develop. The common theme is that wherever the project sits, power, land and skilled people are in high demand. As Southeast Asia's data centre market continues to scale, understanding these cost dynamics will be critical for developers and investors planning their next move in the region," said Patrick Thilagaraj, Project Director - Data Centres, at Turner & Townsend in Malaysia.

The findings also point to a broader rise in project size linked to AI infrastructure. Larger facilities are changing delivery methods and increasing pressure on specialist labour, materials and project risk pricing.

More than half of respondents, 52%, said most of their projects in 2027 are expected to be data centres built to support AI workloads. In 2026, 52% reported cost increases of more than 6%, while about 20% saw increases above 15%.

### Cost pressures

The study suggests cost inflation may be easing, though not disappearing. For 2027, 28% of respondents expect cost increases of between 1% and 5%, while 57% expect rises to remain below 15%.

Labour remains one of the biggest constraints. Some 81% of respondents said skilled labour in their region was either moderately or highly constrained, and only 52% said contractor capacity was manageable.

Power supply was another major issue for new developments. The research found that 56% of respondents identified power as a major obstacle to successful delivery. Meanwhile, 52% said utility connections typically take between one and two years, and 32% said the process takes more than two years.

These delays matter because developers are under pressure to bring new capacity online quickly to meet demand from cloud and AI customers. At the same time, markets with lower upfront construction costs may not offer the same depth of infrastructure or operational experience as more mature hubs.

### Asia focus

Asia is playing a larger role in global data centre investment. The region now includes both the world's most expensive and some of its cheapest construction markets, giving investors a wide range of options depending on land, labour and utility availability.

"Asia is no longer a follower in the global data centre story - it is setting the pace. Tokyo and Osaka lead our index, Singapore sits in the top five, and markets from Hong Kong and Jakarta to Mumbai, Ho Chi Minh City and Shanghai are all seeing sustained investment. That reflects how much capital, and how much confidence, is now flowing into the region as AI, cloud and the need to hold data locally converge. Each market brings something different to that picture. Some offer deep pools of operational experience and established hyperscale demand; others offer greater availability of land, labour and local supply chains, and are growing quickly as a result. Together they give operators and investors a genuine choice about where and how to build. The teams delivering well in Asia are those that plan early, secure the fundamentals up front and bring rigorous cost and risk management in from the very start," said Sumit Mukherjee, Managing Director and Head of Real Estate, Asia, at Turner & Townsend.
